claim: Enpp2/Autotaxin is expressed in GP38+ CD31- FRCs and GP38- CD31+ blood endothelial cells, with negligible expression in lymphatic ECs and double-negative cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, Enpp2/Autotaxin was readily detected in GP38+ CD31- FRCs as well as GP38- CD31+ blood endothelial cells (ECs), with negligible expression in lymphatic ECs and double-negative cells.
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B comparing expression across stromal cell subsets.

claim: ATX is expressed in FRCs surrounding collagen fiber bundles.
source: Electron microscopic analysis confirmed that ATX was expressed in the FRCs surrounding collagen fiber bundles (Figure 1C).
evidence: Confirmed by immunoelectron microscopy images in Figure 1C.

claim: Enpp2 is selectively expressed in LN FRCs but not splenic FRCs.
source: Interestingly, analyses using Ccl19-Cre x R26-EYFP mice, which constitutively express yellow fluorescent protein (YFP) in FRCs (Chai et al., 2013), revealed that Enpp2 was selectively expressed in LN FRCs but not splenic FRCs (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative RT-PCR data from Ccl19-Cre x R26-EYFP mice shown in Figure 1D, and cites previous work by Chai et al., 2013.

claim: Enpp2 expression in FRCs is dependent on LTβR signaling.
source: This Enpp2 expression was apparently dependent on LTβR signaling, because blocking LTβR signaling significantly reduced expression of Enpp2, Cxcl13, and Ccl19, but not Icam1, in FRCs (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by LTβR-Fc blockade experiments showing reduced Enpp2 expression in FRCs, as shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Blocking LTβR signaling downregulates transcription of HEV marker genes such as Glycam1 and Ccl21 in BECs.
source: This blockade also downregulated transcription of HEV marker genes such as Glycam1 and Ccl21 in BECs (Figure 1E), consistent with a previous report (Browning et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figure 1E and consistent with prior findings by Browning et al., 2005.

claim: In Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl mice, Enpp2 is completely lost in FRCs but not in BECs.
source: As expected, in the Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl mice, Enpp2 was completely lost in the FRCs but not in the BECs, whereas Ccl21 and GP38 expression was comparable between these strains (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative RT-PCR data in Figure 2A and flow cytometry in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: LPA (18:0) signals are widely distributed in the LN and are comparable in intensity and frequency between Enpp2fl/fl and Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl mice.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, signals corresponding to LPA (18:0) were widely distributed in the LN. The signals were comparable in intensity and frequency in Enpp2fl/fl and Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl mice; this LPA species appears to be produced mainly within the cell (Aoki, J; unpublished observation) independently of ATX (Yukiura et al., 2011, Nishimasu, et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by imaging mass spectrometry data in Figure 2B and cited studies by Yukiura et al., 2011 and Nishimasu et al., 2011.

claim: LPA (18:1), LPA (18:2), and LPA (20:4) signals are predominantly observed in the paracortex and are substantially decreased in Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl compared with Enpp2fl/fl mice.
source: In sharp contrast, signals corresponding to LPA (18:1), LPA (18:2), and LPA (20:4), the major species produced extracellularly by ATX (Yukiura et al., 2011), were predominantly observed in the paracortex both close to and at a distance from HEVs, but only marginally in the medulla. These signals were substantially decreased in the cortex of Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl as compared with Enpp2fl/fl mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging mass spectrometry in Figure 2B and supported by citation to Yukiura et al., 2011.

claim: The frequency of LPA (18:1), LPA (18:2), and LPA (20:4) signals more than 50 μm from HEVs decreases substantially when ATX is ablated in FRCs.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, the frequency of LPA (18:1), LPA (18:2), and LPA (20:4) signals within 50 μm of an HEV did not differ significantly between Enpp2fl/fl and Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl mice. However, the frequency of relatively distant signals (more than 50 μm) decreased substantially when ATX was ablated in FRCs.
evidence: Quantified by distance measurements from HEVs shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The median distance between LPA signals and HEVs is significantly reduced in Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl compared with Enpp2fl/fl mice.
source: Hence, the median distance between LPA signals and HEVs was significantly reduced in Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl compared with Enpp2fl/fl mice, consistent with the idea that distant LPA signals were associated with FRCs.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2C showing median distance measurements.

claim: Cortical LPA signals not associated with HEVs are mainly produced by FRCs in an ATX-dependent manner.
source: Together with the observations showing robust expression of ATX in FRCs, these findings indicate that the cortical LPA signals not associated with HEVs are mainly produced by FRCs in an ATX-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from combined observations of ATX expression in FRCs and LPA distribution patterns in conditional knockout mice.

claim: CD4+ T-cell movement and displacement from the original location in the PLN is substantially restricted in Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl compared with Enpp2fl/fl mice.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, B, CD4+ T-cell movement and displacement from the original location in the PLN was substantially restricted in Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl compared with Enpp2fl/fl mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by intravital two-photon microscopy tracking data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The median T-cell velocity is lower in Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl than in Enpp2fl/fl mice.
source: The median T-cell velocity was also lower in Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl than in Enpp2fl/fl mice (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantified by velocity measurements from two-photon microscopy shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: T-cell motility is impaired in the LN parenchyma of Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl mice as measured by mean displacement and motility coefficient.
source: Measurement of the mean displacement and the motility coefficient, which represents the volume in which an average cell scans per unit time (Sumen et al., 2004), also indicated that T-cell motility was impaired in the LN parenchyma of Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl mice (Figure 3D,E), whereas the directionality of the intranodal T-cell movement was comparable in these mouse groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), supporting the hypothesis that FRC-derived LPA is required for efficient intranodal T-cell migration.
evidence: Quantified by mean displacement and motility coefficient calculations shown in Figure 3D and 3E, with citation to Sumen et al., 2004 for methodology.

claim: CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and B cells express different levels of Lpar2, Lpar5, and Lpar6, with B cells expressing relatively high levels of Lpar2 compared to T cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and B cells expressed different levels of Lpar2, Lpar5, and Lpar6, encoding LPA2, LPA5 and LPA6 respectively, with B cells expressing relatively high levels of Lpar2 compared to T cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Lpar5-/- and Lpar6-/- lymphocytes migrate into the LN and spleen at levels comparable to WT lymphocytes.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, Lpar5-/- and Lpar6-/- lymphocytes migrated into the LN and spleen at levels comparable to WT lymphocytes.
evidence: Demonstrated by adoptive transfer experiments and flow cytometry shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There are more Lpar2-/- than WT lymphocytes in the LNs but not the spleen.
source: In contrast, there were more Lpar2-/- than WT lymphocytes in the LNs but not the spleen (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Among migrating cells, the increase in Lpar2-/- cells in LNs is evident for CD4+ T cells and CD8+ T cells but not B cells.
source: Among the migrating cells, this increase was evident for CD4+ T cells and CD8+ T cells but not B cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis of lymphocyte subpopulations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Lpar2-/- and WT T cells localize in the vicinity of HEVs (within 50 μm distance) at comparable levels.
source: Among the donor T cells in the LN parenchyma, Lpar2-/- and WT T cells localized in the vicinity of HEVs (within 50 μm distance) at comparable levels (Figure 4E and F), indicating that LPA2 plays a minor role in T cell entry into LNs across HEVs.
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and distance measurements shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: Lpar2-/- T cells localize more frequently in areas distant (more than 50 μm away) from HEVs compared with WT T cells.
source: By contrast, Lpar2-/- T cells localized more frequently in the area distant (more than 50 μm away) from HEVs compared with WT T cells (Figure 4E and F), consistent with the hypothesis that LPA promotes intranodal T cell migration via LPA2, and hence, Lpar2-deficient T cells were retained in the LN parenchyma.
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and distance measurements shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: Blockade of T cell entry results in an increased ratio of Lpar2-/- T cells to WT cells in LNs 23 hr after injection.
source: As shown in Figure 4G, the blockade of T cell entry (T = 23 hr) resulted in reduction of the cellularity in LNs and increased the ratio of Lpar2-/- T cells to WT cells compared to that before the injection.
evidence: Demonstrated by L-selectin blockade experiments and flow cytometry shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Lpar2-/- T cells have a 13% lower average velocity than WT T cells.
source: Lpar2-/- T cells had a 13% lower average velocity (Figure 5B), a 45% lower mean square displacement (Figure 5C), and a 70% lower motility coefficient than WT T cells (Figure 5D), although the directionality of T-cell motion was comparable in these cell types (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantified by intravital two-photon microscopy measurements shown in Figure 5B, 5C, and 5D.

claim: In Enpp2fl/fl mice, Lpar2-/- T cells have significantly less intranodal motility than WT cells.
source: In Enpp2fl/fl mice, Lpar2-/- T cells had significantly less intranodal motility than WT cells (Figure 5E,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by two-photon microscopy in Enpp2fl/fl mice shown in Figure 5E and 5G.

claim: Reduced intranodal motility of Lpar2-/- T cells is not observed in Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl mice, which lack ATX/LPA in the FRCs.
source: On the other hand, a reduced intranodal motility of Lpar2-/- T cells was not observed in Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl mice, which lack ATX/LPA in the FRCs (Figure 5F,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by two-photon microscopy in Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl mice shown in Figure 5F and 5G.

claim: Intranodal T-cell motility is regulated via LPA2 on T cells and requires FRC-derived LPA.
source: These results indicate that intranodal T-cell motility is regulated via LPA2 on T cells and that the LPA2-mediated T-cell motility requires FRC-derived LPA.
evidence: Inferred from combined results of experiments in Enpp2fl/fl and Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl mice.

claim: Blockade of LFA-1/ICAM-1 interaction significantly attenuates WT T cell motility.
source: As shown in Figure 5H–J and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C–E, the blockade of the interaction between LFA-1 and ICAM-1 significantly attenuated WT T cell motility as reported previously (Katakai et al., 2013; Woolf et al., 2007).
evidence: Demonstrated by anti-LFA-1 antibody blockade experiments shown in Figure 5H-J, with citations to Katakai et al., 2013 and Woolf et al., 2007.

claim: Even in the absence of LFA-1/ICAM-1 interaction, Lpar2 deficiency reduces T-cell motility to a comparable extent as in the presence of integrin interaction.
source: Of note, even in the absence of the LFA-1/ICAM-1 interaction, Lpar2 deficiency reduced T-cell motility, and the extent of reduction in T-cell velocity (19.9 ± 5.5%) and motility coefficient (43.5 ± 16.8%) was comparable to that observed in the presence of the integrin interaction (15.8 ± 4.4% and 43.0 ± 13.6% reduction in velocity and motility coefficient, respectively) (Figure 5H–J and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C–E).
evidence: Quantified by velocity and motility coefficient measurements with and without LFA-1 blockade shown in Figure 5H-J.

claim: LPA/LPA2 regulates T-cell motility at least partly in an integrin-independent manner.
source: These results support the hypothesis that LPA/LPA2 regulates T-cell motility at least partly in an integrin-independent manner.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing comparable effects of Lpar2 deficiency with and without LFA-1 blockade.

claim: LPA-pretreated WT T cells have a higher velocity and a smaller mean turning angle compared to untreated WT T cells in 2D migration toward CCL21.
source: As shown in Figure 6A,B, WT T cells efficiently migrated toward CCL21 in response to LPA in a time-dependent manner. Compared to untreated WT T cells, LPA-sensitized WT T cells had a higher velocity and a smaller mean turning angle (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by EZ-Taxiscan chamber experiments shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: LPA treatment does not enhance the migration of Lpar2-/- T cells toward CCL21 in 2D environment.
source: In contrast, LPA treatment did not enhance the migration of Lpar2-/- T cells toward CCL21.
evidence: Demonstrated by EZ-Taxiscan chamber experiments comparing WT and Lpar2-/- T cells.

claim: LPA sensitization enhances CD4+ T cell migration across 3-μm pore filters, and this enhancement is strongly inhibited by ROCK inhibitor Y27632.
source: As shown in Figure 7A, LPA sensitization enhanced the migration of CD4+ T cells, and this enhancement was strongly inhibited by the ROCK inhibitor Y27632 (Figure 7A), or the myosin II ATPase inhibitor blebbistatin (Figure 7B), but not by pertussis toxin (PTX), which inhibits Gαi signaling (Figure 7A).
evidence: Demonstrated by Transwell migration assays with inhibitors shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: At 1 μM, LPA prominently induces chemokinesis in WT CD4+T cells but not in Lpar2-/- CD4+ T cells.
source: At 1 μM, LPA prominently induced chemokinesis in WT CD4+T cells, consistent with previous reports (Kanda et al., 2008; Katakai et al., 2014) (Figure 7C), but this effect was not observed in Lpar2-/- CD4+ T cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Transwell assays shown in Figure 7C, with citations to Kanda et al., 2008 and Katakai et al., 2014.

claim: LPA induces RhoA activation in WT but not Lpar2-/- CD4+ T cells.
source: As shown in Figure 7D and E, LPA induced RhoA activation in WT but not Lpar2-/- CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by RhoA-GTP pull-down assays shown in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: LPA noticeably enhances CCL21-dependent migration of T cells across 3-μm- but not 5-μm-pore diameter filters.
source: Reminiscent of the findings of Soriano et al for ROCK/myosin II signaling (Soriano et al., 2011), LPA noticeably enhanced the CCL21-dependent migration of T cells across a 3-μm- but not 5-μm-pore diameter filter (Figure 7F), and that Lpar2 deficiency abolished the LPA-induced enhancement (Figure 7G).
evidence: Demonstrated by Transwell assays with different pore sizes shown in Figure 7F and 7G, with citation to Soriano et al., 2011.

claim: LPA limits T-cell adhesion area on fibronectin- or ICAM-1-coated substrate in WT T cells, which is inhibited by blebbistatin treatment.
source: As shown in Figure 8A,B, and D, LPA limited T-cell adhesion area on the fibronectin- or ICAM-1-coated substrate in WT T cells, which was inhibited by treatment of cells with blebbistatin, but this effect was not observed in Lpar2-/- T cells, suggesting that Lpar2-/- T cells over-adhere to substrate coated with or without LFA-1 ligand.
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy measurements shown in Figure 8A, 8B, and 8D.

claim: LPA/LPA2 signaling induces T-cell elongation in a myosin II-dependent manner.
source: Consistently, the LPA/LPA2 signaling induced T-cell elongation in a myosin II-dependent manner, allowing swift cell movement (Figure 8A, C, E).
evidence: Demonstrated by morphology measurements (aspect ratio and circularity) shown in Figure 8A, 8C, and 8E.

claim: WT T cells efficiently migrate toward CCL21 in the presence of LPA in 3D collagen gel, with increased displacement and velocity compared with cells stimulated with CCL21 alone.
source: WT T cells efficiently migrated toward CCL21 in the presence of LPA, with increased displacement (Figure 9B) and velocity (Figure 9C) compared with cells stimulated with CCL21 alone, whereas the directionality of T cell movement in the gel was comparable in the presence or absence of LPA (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D collagen gel migration assays shown in Figure 9B and 9C.

claim: LPA's effect on T cell migration in 3D collagen gel is abrogated by treatment with Y27632 or blebbistatin.
source: The LPA's effect was abrogated by treatment of the cells with Y27632 or blebbistatin (Figure 9D).
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D collagen gel migration assays with inhibitors shown in Figure 9D.

claim: In Lpar2-/- T cells, CCL21 does not enhance motility in the presence of LPA in 3D collagen gel.
source: In Lpar2-/- T cells, CCL21 did not enhance motility in the presence of LPA (Figure 9B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D collagen gel migration assays comparing WT and Lpar2-/- T cells shown in Figure 9B and 9C.

claim: In confined 3D environments, the LPA-LPA2 axis regulates T-cell motility in a manner dependent on Rho, ROCK, and actomyosin.
source: These results collectively indicate that in confined 3D environments, the LPA-LPA2 axis regulates T-cell motility in a manner dependent on Rho, ROCK, and actomyosin.
evidence: Inferred from combined results of 3D migration assays with inhibitors and genetic knockouts.

claim: FRC-derived LPA is essential for LPA2-dependent T-cell motility in densely packed LN parenchyma.
source: LPA produced by FRCs is essential for this LPA2-dependent T-cell motility in densely packed LN parenchyma.
evidence: Inferred from combined results showing FRC-specific ATX deletion reduces LPA and impairs T cell motility.

claim: Multiple biologically relevant LPA species (18:1, 18:2, 20:4) are produced by FRCs.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that multiple biologically relevant LPA species (18:1, 18:2, 20:4) are produced by FRCs, which may in turn act locally on LPA receptors expressed by adjacent lymphocytes.
evidence: Inferred from imaging mass spectrometry data showing these LPA species in FRC-rich areas.

claim: LPA acts on LPA2 to enhance T-cell motility in chemokine-rich, confined environments at least partly independently of integrin-mediated adhesion or de-adhesion.
source: These findings indicate that LPA acts on LPA2 to enhance T-cell motility in chemokine-rich, confined environments at least partly independently of integrin-mediated adhesion or de-adhesion, and this enhancement depends mainly on ROCK/myosin IIA activity.
evidence: Inferred from combined in vitro and in vivo experiments showing LPA effects persist with LFA-1 blockade.

claim: FRC-derived LPA signals T cells through LPA2 to sustain optimal T-cell motility in the LN parenchyma.
source: We further demonstrated that FRC-derived LPA signaled T cells through LPA2 to sustain optimal T-cell motility in the LN parenchyma.
evidence: Inferred from combined results of conditional knockout and receptor-deficient mice experiments.

claim: LPA serves as a cell-extrinsic factor regulating myosin II activity in CD4+ T cells.
source: Thus, LPA appears to serve as a cell-extrinsic factor regulating myosin II activity in CD4+ T cells, and the LPA2/ROCK/myosin II signaling pathway is critical for T-cell migration in the confined LN parenchymal environment.
evidence: Inferred from combined results showing LPA activates RhoA/ROCK/myosin II pathway and affects T cell motility in confined environments.

claim: LPA locally produced by HEV ECs regulates constitutive lymphocyte transmigration across HEVs.
source: We and others previously reported that LPA locally produced by HEV ECs regulates constitutive lymphocyte transmigration across HEVs (Bai et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Cites previous studies by Bai et al., 2013 and Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: LPA enhances lymphocyte detachment from ECs and promotes lymphocyte transmigration across the HEV basal lamina, at least in part by acting on HEV ECs.
source: We also demonstrated that LPA enhances lymphocyte detachment from ECs and promotes lymphocyte transmigration across the HEV basal lamina, at least in part by acting on HEV ECs (Bai et al., 2013).
evidence: Cites previous study by Bai et al., 2013.

claim: LPA acts on naïve T cells to induce chemokinesis and cell polarization.
source: LPA also acts on naïve T cells to induce chemokinesis and cell polarization (Kanda et al., 2008; Katakai et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2012) and transmigration (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Cites previous studies by Kanda et al., 2008, Katakai et al., 2014, and Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: A study using pharmacological inhibitors revealed that ATX/LPA promotes intranodal lymphocyte motility in an ex vivo LN explant model.
source: While a study using pharmacological inhibitors revealed that ATX/LPA promotes intranodal lymphocyte motility in an ex vivo LN explant model (Katakai et al., 2014), the physiological significance of the ATX/LPA axis in interstitial lymphocyte migration remains unknown.
evidence: Cites previous study by Katakai et al., 2014.

claim: Six LPA receptors (LPA1–LPA6) have been identified.
source: To date, six LPA receptors (LPA1–LPA6) have been identified.
evidence: Represents established scientific knowledge about LPA receptors.

claim: LPA receptors couple to multiple G proteins, including Gi, G12/13, Gq, and Gs.
source: LPA receptors couple to multiple G proteins, including Gi, G12/13, Gq, and Gs, and upon ligand binding, these G proteins activate diverse intracellular signaling components including Rho and Rac.
evidence: Represents established scientific knowledge about LPA receptor signaling.

claim: LPA2 has been reported to play a role in intranodal T-cell migration.
source: Although LPA2 has recently been reported to play a role in intranodal T-cell migration (Knowlden et al., 2014), it remains unclear how LPA2-mediated signaling affects interstitial T-cell motility and whether LPA is the prime activating ligand.
evidence: Cites previous study by Knowlden et al., 2014.

claim: Leukocyte migration in a confined environment is regulated at least partly by cell contraction.
source: Leukocyte migration in a confined environment is regulated at least partly by cell contraction (Lämmermann et al., 2008).
evidence: Cites previous study by Lämmermann et al., 2008.

claim: Myosin IIA is required for T-cell amoeboid motility in confined environments such as LNs.
source: Jacobelli et al. (2010) reported that a contractile protein, myosin IIA, is required for T-cell amoeboid motility in confined environments such as LNs (Jacobelli et al., 2010).
evidence: Cites previous study by Jacobelli et al., 2010.

claim: Myosin IIA cross-links actin, thus limiting surface adhesion and allowing T cells to exert contractile force.
source: Myosin IIA cross-links actin, thus limiting surface adhesion and allowing T cells to exert contractile force.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about myosin IIA function.

claim: Myosin IIA's activity is regulated by RhoA and Rho-associated protein kinase (ROCK) signaling.
source: Myosin IIA's activity is regulated by RhoA and Rho-associated protein kinase (ROCK) signaling.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about myosin IIA regulation.

claim: LPA induces cell polarization in zebrafish germ progenitor cells in a ROCK-myosin II-dependent manner, enabling rapid cell migration in a confined environment.
source: While the cell-extrinsic factor(s) that regulate myosin II's activity during T-cell migration in a confined environment have been poorly defined, a recent study using zebrafish germ progenitor cells showed that LPA induces cell polarization in a ROCK-myosin II-dependent manner, which enables rapid cell migration in a confined environment (Ruprecht et al., 2015).
evidence: Cites previous study by Ruprecht et al., 2015.

claim: Blood-borne naïve lymphocytes migrate along the fibroblastic reticular cell (FRC) network in lymph nodes (LNs).
source: Blood-borne naïve lymphocytes migrate along the fibroblastic reticular cell (FRC) network in lymph nodes (LNs) (von Andrian and Mempel, 2003; Miyasaka and Tanaka, 2004; Girard et al., 2012).
evidence: Cites previous studies by von Andrian and Mempel, 2003, Miyasaka and Tanaka, 2004, and Girard et al., 2012.

claim: B cells migrate into LN follicles, whereas T cells remain in the paracortex and migrate continually along the FRC network.
source: B cells then migrate into LN follicles, whereas T cells remain in the paracortex and migrate continually along the FRC network (Bajénoff et al., 2006).
evidence: Cites previous study by Bajénoff et al., 2006.

claim: Naïve T cells crawl along the FRC network in an apparently random pattern of motion, at an average velocity of 10–15 μm per minute.
source: Two-photon microscopic analysis has shown that naïve T cells crawl along the FRC network in an apparently random pattern of motion, at an average velocity of 10–15 μm per minute (Miller et al., 2002; Okada and Cyster, 2007; Worbs et al., 2007).
evidence: Cites previous studies by Miller et al., 2002, Okada and Cyster, 2007, and Worbs et al., 2007.

claim: FRCs promote intranodal T-cell motility by signaling naïve lymphocytes with CCL21/CCL19 via CCR7, thus activating the small GTPase Rac.
source: FRCs promote intranodal T-cell motility by signaling naïve lymphocytes with CCL21/CCL19 via CCR7, thus activating the small GTPase Rac (Okada and Cyster, 2007; Worbs et al., 2007; Faroudi et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2007), although CCR7 signaling only partially account for the interstitial T cell motility (Okada and Cyster, 2007; Huang et al., 2007).
evidence: Cites previous studies by Okada and Cyster, 2007, Worbs et al., 2007, Faroudi et al., 2010, and Huang et al., 2007.

claim: LPA is a bioactive lysophospholipid produced both extracellularly and intracellularly.
source: LPA is a bioactive lysophospholipid produced both extracellularly and intracellularly.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about LPA.

claim: Extracellularly produced LPA is involved in diverse biological functions including vascular remodeling and cell growth, survival, and migration.
source: Extracellularly produced LPA is involved in such diverse biological functions as vascular remodeling and cell growth, survival, and migration (Choi et al., 2010; Yanagida et al., 2013).
evidence: Cites previous studies by Choi et al., 2010 and Yanagida et al., 2013.

claim: Intracellularly produced LPA is an intermediate in the synthesis of triglycerides and glycerophospholipids, and is thought to act as a 'housekeeper' inside the cell.
source: Intracellularly produced LPA is an intermediate in the synthesis of triglycerides and glycerophospholipids, and thought to act as a 'housekeeper' inside the cell (Mills and Moolenaar, 2003).
evidence: Cites previous study by Mills and Moolenaar, 2003.

claim: Extracellular LPA is predominantly produced by autotaxin (ATX), an ectoenzyme originally identified as a tumor-cell motility-enhancing factor.
source: Extracellular LPA is predominantly produced by autotaxin (ATX, also referred to as ENPP2 [ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase family member 2]), an ectoenzyme that was originally identified as a tumor-cell motility-enhancing factor (Stracke et al., 1992).
evidence: Cites previous study by Stracke et al., 1992.

claim: ATX is a lysophospholipase D that produces LPA by hydrolyzing lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC).
source: ATX is a lysophospholipase D that produces LPA by hydrolyzing lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) (Okudaira et al., 2010; Moolenaar and Perrakis, 2011).
evidence: Cites previous studies by Okudaira et al., 2010 and Moolenaar and Perrakis, 2011.

claim: ATX is strongly expressed in HEV endothelial cells and regulates lymphocyte migration into the LN parenchyma.
source: We and others have reported that ATX is strongly expressed in HEV endothelial cells (ECs), and that ATX regulates lymphocyte migration into the LN parenchyma (Kanda et al., 2008; Nakasaki et al., 2008; Umemoto et al., 2011).
evidence: Cites previous studies by Kanda et al., 2008, Nakasaki et al., 2008, and Umemoto et al., 2011.

claim: Recombinant mouse ATX prefers LPC species with relatively short, unsaturated acyl chains, and produces LPA (18:2), LPA (16:0), LPA (20:4), and LPA (18:1) but not LPA (18:0).
source: Recombinant mouse ATX prefers LPC species with relatively short, unsaturated acyl chains, and produces LPA (18:2), LPA (16:0), LPA (20:4), and LPA (18:1) but not LPA (18:0) (Yukiura et al., 2011).
evidence: Cites previous study by Yukiura et al., 2011.

claim: Crystal structural analysis revealed that ATX accommodates LPA (18:1) and LPA (18:3) but not LPA (18:0) in a stable conformation in its hydrophobic pocket.
source: Consistent with this observation, crystal structural analysis revealed that ATX accommodates LPA (18:1) and LPA (18:3) but not LPA (18:0) in a stable conformation in its hydrophobic pocket, accounting for ATX's preferences for the number of unsaturated bonds of LPC (18:0 < 18:1 < 18:3) (Nishimasu et al., 2011).
evidence: Cites previous study by Nishimasu et al., 2011.

claim: LPA (18:0) is relatively inert in activating LPA receptors.
source: While LPA (18:0) signals were detected in the LN parenchyma, they were ubiquitously found in other tissues independently of ATX expression; these signals are likely to represent intracellularly produced LPA, an intermediate in the synthesis of triglycerides and glycerophospholipids inside the cell (Mills and Moolenaar, 2003), which is relatively inert in activating LPA receptors (Bandoh et al., 2000).
evidence: Cites previous studies by Mills and Moolenaar, 2003 and Bandoh et al., 2000.

claim: Lymphocyte migration across a filter with a 3-μm pore diameter depends on ROCK/myosin II signaling, while migration across a 5-μm pore does not.
source: Transwell analyses have shown that lymphocyte migration across a filter with a 3-μm pore diameter depends on ROCK/myosin II signaling, while migration across a 5-μm pore does not (Soriano et al., 2011).
evidence: Cites previous study by Soriano et al., 2011.

claim: TCR activation downregulates LPA2 expression.

evidence: Cites previous study by Mandl et al., 2012.

claim: Ccl19-Cre mice express transgenes in FRCs and in the mesenchymal cells ensheathing HEV ECs, but not in HEV ECs.
source: Given that Ccl19-Cre mice express transgenes in FRCs and in the mesenchymal cells ensheathing HEV ECs, but not in HEV ECs (Chai et al., 2013), and that biologically relevant LPA species were produced near HEVs at comparable levels in Ccl19-Cre Enpp2fl/fl mice and Enpp2fl/fl mice (Figure 2B,C), it appears that ATX produced outside HEVs plays a minor or dispensable role in the lymphocyte transmigration across HEVs.
evidence: Inferred from Ccl19-Cre expression pattern cited from Chai et al., 2013 and LPA distribution data in Figure 2B,C.
